title: LLM Quality Optimization Bootcamp: Thierry Moreau and Pedro Torruella
talk_summary: A vendor-led bootcamp on fine-tuning small open models (Llama 3 8B with LoRA) for a narrow, high-volume task (PII redaction via function calling), claiming 47% better accuracy and ~200x cost reduction vs GPT-4. The transferable core is not fine-tuning itself but the discipline around it: narrow task scoping, logged input/output pairs as training data, train/val/test splits, and programmatic pass/fail accuracy metrics against ground truth.

takeaways.technique: Programmatic ground-truth scoring instead of LLM-as-judge
takeaways.what_they_do: For tasks with labeled ground truth they score outputs with a deterministic metric (penalizing false positives/negatives, fuzzy match on labels) rather than asking an LLM to grade, avoiding self-preference bias.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we don't have to use an llm for instance for that we can actually use more traditional techniques of accuracy evaluation
takeaways.numbers: fine-tune 0.97 vs GPT-4 0.68 average accuracy on 100 samples

takeaways.what_they_do: They insist on holding out data the model never saw and a third test set for real-world examples, so evaluation isn't contaminated by training data.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you want to split your data set into a training and validation um set because you don't want to evaluate your model on data that your um fine-tune has seen

takeaways.technique: Narrow-task small model with LoRA instead of frontier model
takeaways.what_they_do: For a single well-scoped task (classification/extraction/function-calling) they fine-tune a small open model with parameter-efficient LoRA and serve many LoRAs per GPU, rather than calling a frontier model.
takeaways.evidence_quote: for very specialized task which is we going to look at today like classification or labeling or function calling a Laura is just fine
takeaways.numbers: ~$0.15/M tokens vs ~$30/M tokens; 50MB LoRA vs 15GB checkpoint

takeaways.what_they_do: They frame fine-tuning as a last resort after prompt engineering and RAG, and only when the task is narrow and you own high-quality data.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it's not really a silver bullet for all the problems you're going to face but one used right in the right context for the right problem it can really deliver results

takeaways.technique: Log real input/output pairs as a reusable dataset
takeaways.what_they_do: They capture production prompts and responses (system prompt + tools + user + expected tool call) as JSONL training samples, so the same logs serve evaluation and future tuning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you need to make it seem like you've essentially logged conversations with an llm right you're logging the prompts and the responses
takeaways.numbers: 10,000 training samples built from a 200k dataset

takeaways.technique: Task-specific model selection by cost/quality quadrant
takeaways.what_they_do: They explicitly map the cost-vs-quality tradeoff and argue for moving from high-cost/low-quality prototypes to low-cost/high-quality production by matching model size to task narrowness.
takeaways.evidence_quote: to go to production you need to end on the opposite quadrant right lower cost higher quality
takeaways.numbers: 47% better accuracy at 99.5% lower cost claimed
